ansel:gecco:2011: Outside those descendants, external reception is thin. The most substantive notice comes from the autotuning community itself: Basu, Hall, and colleagues discuss the algorithm in their account of making autotuning mainstream, treating it as one of the field's evolutionary search strategies. Later tuners such as Bliss, and work on parallel iterative compilation, cite it only in passing. The paper's reception is hard to separate from the PetaBricks project it served; read on its own, it is a technique noted by close neighbors rather than one taken up beyond them. The PetaBricks implementation is preserved in the petabricks/petabricks repository.
amarasinghe:cgo:2005: What traveled is the argument rather than any artifact. The small citing literature invokes the keynote almost entirely as evidence: the pipeline-parallelism line of Giacomoni, Vachharajani, and colleagues, from FastForward through its companion reports, cites it for the premise that multicores shift the burden of performance onto software, and work on visualizing potential parallelism and on teaching multicore programming uses it the same way. Every judged citation is peripheral, and none builds on the talk itself — the expected shape for a keynote abstract whose diagnosis was becoming common ground. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure underlying the talk's third case study lives on in bthies/streamit.
tiramisu-li: The citation record is thin and uniformly brief. The paper appears in passing in the related work of later efforts in the same line — Pearl's reinforcement-learning code optimization, a cost model supporting dynamic program sizes, a reinforcement-learning environment for the MLIR compiler, CHEHAB's homomorphic-encryption optimization — and in a survey of lightweight deep learning, as one instance of a learned compiler heuristic. No citing work engages the model in depth; its reception is as an entry in the catalogue of neural approaches to loop optimization. An archival artifact accompanies the paper on Zenodo.
arxiv:2506.11021: The preprint's citation record is small and entirely peripheral. Such engagement as exists comes from work on estimating the correctness of generated code: papers on ensemble-based uncertainty estimation and on predicting program correctness by ensemble semantic entropy discuss the clustering approach in some detail, a paper on semantic collapse in coding models cites it as an example, and a study of optimal reasoning length for RL-trained language models takes up one of its ideas. Evaluations of hallucination in generative AI systems mention it in passing. This is reception at the registration stage: the method is noticed and named rather than built on.
randomwalk-iiswc21: The citing literature is small but concrete. The open-source implementations found users: work on sparsifying graph neural networks, including a compressive-sensing variant, builds on them, and Towards Real-Time Temporal Graph Learning measures against the paper's characterization. GENTI, a GPU system for walk-based subgraph extraction, positions itself relative to the study, and Mint's accelerator for temporal motif mining cites its findings on workload behavior. The remaining citations are passing mentions in papers on graph accelerators and temporal graph learning, where the characterization appears as background rather than as a result in use. The implementations are available at talnish/iiswc21_rwalk, with an archival artifact deposited on Zenodo.
bosboom:oopsla:2014: External take-up of the commensal approach is limited. LaminarIR, with its compile-time queues for structured streams, measures its performance against StreamJIT, and that is the one sustained engagement in the record. The other citations are list placements: RaftLib and Streams a la carte name StreamJIT among stream programming systems, and an application of OpenTuner to GPU compiler parameters lists it among systems that delegate tuning decisions to OpenTuner. The record is small enough that reception reads as recognition among stream-language designers rather than adoption of commensal compilation elsewhere. The implementation lives in jbosboom/streamjit on GitHub.
askit-cgo24: The citation record is thin and almost entirely peripheral. Works on prompt programming and LLM-driven code generation — APPL and DSL-Xpert among them — cite AskIt in passing as one of the languages for integrating LLM calls into programs, and a survey of interaction techniques in generative AI applications lists it alongside other interfaces. The remaining mentions come from applied LLM papers on subjects from malware deobfuscation to financial forecasting, citing it briefly for context. None of the judged citations engages the DSL's mechanisms in depth; the reception is list membership in a broad literature on programming with language models. The TypeScript and Python implementations live at katsumiok/ts-askit and katsumiok/pyaskit, and an archival evaluation artifact accompanies the paper.
seq-nature-biotech: Reception of the correspondence itself is small but concrete. The citations that engage it come from tools: a framework for characterizing segmental duplication structure across genome assemblies is written in Seq, Sequre builds secure multiparty computation for biomedical data sharing on top of it, and Vectron uses its infrastructure for auto-vectorized dynamic programming. Other genomics work, including minimizer-space assembly and the mapquik read mapper, cites it when arguing that performance-minded tooling matters in the field. Much of the small external record is unjudged, so the fuller picture is uncertain, but the judged citations are the kind a language wants: people writing software in it. The language lives on at seq-lang/seq and, under the Codon umbrella, at exaloop/seq.
buildsl-cgo22: Outside those two lines the citation record is thin. A few external works cite the paper briefly: a systematic literature review of DSLs for algorithmic graph processing includes it, eCC++ names it as an instance of compiler construction for embedded DSLs, and Flan's Datalog compiler mentions it in passing among staging-based systems. None engages the staging argument in depth; the case the paper makes is carried mainly by the group's own successor systems rather than by external uptake. An archival artifact accompanies the paper.
gladshtein_mechanised_2024: Reception comes from the community mechanising relational and hyper program logics. The closest engagement is the authors' own: Lazy Proof Automation for Separation Logic builds on the mechanisation itself, and Foundational Multi-Modal Program Verifiers carries the logic forward. Beyond that line, Barthe's account of the formalization of security discusses the logic at some length, and deductive-verification work on hyper Hoare logics — Hypra and Hyper Separation Logic among them — records LGTM among the relational separation logics it relates to. The citations are few, but they sit squarely in the hypersafety-verification conversation the paper joined. The Coq mechanisation is preserved as an archival artifact on Zenodo.
tseng:ics:1995: The citation record is small, and its judged portion is concentrated: the Kandemir–Ramanujam–Choudhary line on locality optimization cites the paper's findings as supporting evidence — that analyses a distributed-memory compiler must perform pay off as optimizations on shared-memory machines — and Tseng's own later work carries the argument forward. The rest are scattered passing mentions, in HPF benchmark compilation and software-cache management among them. Modest as it is, the record fits the paper's character: a position piece whose measurements are cited as evidence rather than a system to be built on.
arxiv:2005.04091: The preprint's citation trail is short and largely peripheral. The most substantive engagement comes from MLIR's sparse tensor compilation work, which names it as an example of a compiler treating sparsity in deep learning; the remaining citations — PIT's work on dynamic sparse models, a data-centric optimization framework for machine learning, a neural-network pruning study, and a survey of distributed AI — mention it in passing. The paper's role was demonstrative, and its influence is better read through the Tiramisu project it extended than through its own citation record.
thies:bmc:2007: Reception of the article is thin and lies outside the group's usual territory. CONCORD, a consensus method for secondary-structure prediction via mixed-integer linear optimization, engages it in detail; a later study of convolutional networks for secondary-structure prediction mentions it in passing; and two works on structured prediction of matching and degree-constrained graphs cite it as an application of the underlying learning machinery. The few substantive mentions treat it as one entry among predictors that work without external databases — a contribution absorbed quietly into the secondary-structure literature rather than one that started a line.
ugcf-isca21: External citation is sparse and clusters around the architectures UGC targets. Work in the HammerBlade line uses the compiler — the paper on supporting dynamic task parallelism on manycore architectures builds with it, and the HammerBlade manycore paper lists it among the software the machine runs — while compiler papers such as MeshTaichi, a multi-target multi-paradigm DSL compiler for algorithmic graph processing, and a tensor processing framework for CPU-manycore heterogeneous systems give it closer readings as a point of comparison for multi-backend design. A systematic literature review of graph-processing DSLs records it among the languages of the field. The compiler lives on in the GraphIt-DSL/graphit repository.
chou:2022:dynamic-formats: Its citations are few and sit at the edges of their papers, coming from the sparse-compilation community the TACO line addresses. The structured-tensor-algebra work of Ghorbani, Bauer, and Grosser engages it most directly, discussing the node-schema approach while compressing structured tensors; WingSpan, Bonsai, and work on optimizing sparse tensor compilation for sparse output cite it as an instance of what format-general compilers cover; a paper on exploiting sparsity in convolutional networks on GPUs cites a finding as evidence. None of the judged citations builds on the system itself, so the paper functions as a boundary marker — cited to note that mutable, pointer-based sparse structures are within a compiler's reach. The implementation lives in the tensor-compiler/taco repository, and an evaluated artifact accompanies the paper.
thies:acm-sigarch-news:2002: Direct citation of the position paper is scant; the argument it distills belongs to the project's language and compiler papers, which carry the fuller treatment. Of the handful of external citations, one is substantive: work on disjoint-path routing for streaming applications uses the StreamIt infrastructure in the tiled-architecture setting the paper describes. Generating stream-based code from plain C positions its recovery of streaming structure against StreamIt's explicit approach, and the rest are passing mentions. The paper's role is best read through the compiler line it argued for, which lives on in the StreamIt compiler infrastructure at bthies/streamit.
kiriansky-pact18-cimple: Outside the group's own follow-on work the citation record is small and concentrated where the paper aimed: the literature on hiding memory latency in in-memory databases. Studies of interleaving with coroutines in index joins and of cooperative multitasking in main-memory database systems cite Cimple's measurements as evidence for software latency-hiding, as do SHADOW's asymmetric-thread architecture and work on harvesting sub-microsecond CXL memory stalls. Systems that chose other routes define themselves against it — Cuckoo Trie for DRAM indexing, Phloem for fine-grain pipeline parallelism in hardware. The volume is limited, but the engagement comes from the community working the same problem.
taco-lossless-cgo22: External reception beyond that lineage is thin, and most of it is passing: papers on compressed set representations, grammar-compressed matrix multiplication, entropy decoding for sparse kernels on GPUs, and kernel generation for quantized language models mention the paper when noting that computation can proceed without decompression. The one detailed external engagement, on optimizing compression schemes for parallel sparse tensor algebra, works through the technique itself, and WingSpan cites its results in support. The idea's clearest continuation runs inside its own line rather than through the external record. The implementation lives in the tensor-compiler/taco repository.
ahrens_finch_2025: The citing record is small, and its closest reader comes from within the project: WingSpan builds concurrency and dependence analysis for sparse and structured tensor compilers on Finch. Outside it, TENSURE's fuzzing work on sparse tensor compilers treats Finch as a compiler to measure against, and work on compressing structured tensor algebra and on optimizing sparse tensor compilation for sparse output positions its own approach against Finch's handling of structure and control flow. The remaining mentions are brief placements among sparse tensor compilers. The compiler lives on in finch-tensor/Finch.jl, and a reusable, reproduced artifact accompanies the paper.
thies:prib:2006: The workshop version drew only a handful of citations, all peripheral. Later work on protein structure prediction — support-vector-machine applications and neural-network fold recognition among them — cites it when reviewing prior secondary-structure methods, sometimes describing the HM-SVM approach at some length, but never building on it directly. The thin record is consistent with the expanded journal article serving as the main point of entry to the work, leaving the workshop paper a minor trace in the citation graph.
revec-cc: The record of citations is thin, and much of it is brief. What gets reused is the benchmark suite: the study of vector processing for mobile devices and work combining run-time checks with compile-time analysis for control-flow auto-vectorization both draw on Revec's intrinsic-rich kernels. Elsewhere Revec appears as an example in work on moving vectorized code across instruction sets — the Lasagne static binary translator and a survey of MIMD execution on SIMD machines cite it in that role — and a journal article on code rejuvenation from vector intrinsics to portable standardized SIMD carries the rejuvenation framing forward. No external system extends the pass itself. The implementation and benchmark suite live in the revec organization on GitHub, as revec/llvm-revec and revec/VectorBench respectively.
thies:mm:2009: External reception of the technique is thin. The works that cite it are mostly surveys and adjacent literature: a survey of compression-domain image and video processing places it as the lossless entry in its map of the area, the Foundations and Trends treatment of pattern matching in compressed texts and images notes it, and Kremlin gives it one of the record's few detailed readings. The idea of computing directly on LZ77-compressed data traveled mainly along the path the summary describes — into the compiler unifying lossless compression with sparse computing — rather than through independent adopters. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure underlying this work lives on in bthies/streamit.
mueller_sparse_2020: Reception is quiet and specific, confined to the sparse tensor systems community. ALTO and the work on compiling modular and general sparse workspaces cite its findings as supporting evidence, and one successor engages head-on: On Higher-performance Sparse Tensor Transposition positions its own algorithms directly against Quesadilla. The remaining references are brief mentions in work on sparsity-aware tensor decomposition, data layout for sparse tensor kernels on GPUs, and autoscheduling for sparse frameworks. The citations are few, as befits a brief announcement, but the closest reader is the one trying to transpose tensors faster. The Quesadilla implementation lives in the tensor-compiler/taco repository.
